questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the word 'stupa' in Sanskrit, and what was its earliest physical form before stone elaboration?
questions.a: 'Stupa' means 'a heap'; the earliest form was a simple semi-circular mound of earth called anda. A wrong answer (e.g., 'stupa means a tower' or 'earliest form was a square platform') reveals confusion with later shikhara temples or a failure to grasp the funerary-mound origin.

questions.q: Why did the Buddha initially discourage honouring his remains but later permit stupas at four crossroads? Explain using the Mahaparinibbana Sutta.
questions.a: The Buddha first told Ananda not to hinder themselves by honouring his remains, but when pressed he allowed stupas at crossroads so that laypeople placing garlands or saluting there would gain long-term merit and joy. A wrong answer (e.g., 'the Buddha wanted monuments for himself') misses the doctrinal shift: stupas serve the laity's merit-making, not the Buddha's glorification.

questions.q: A donative inscription at Sanchi reads: 'Gateway donated by the guild of ivory workers from Vidisha.' What does this single inscription reveal about (a) patronage, (b) economic organisation, and (c) the stupa's social role?
questions.a: (a) Non-royal corporate groups funded major components; (b) craft guilds were wealthy and organised enough to sponsor monumental architecture; (c) the stupa functioned as a public institution integrating diverse social groups. A wrong answer focusing only on 'ivory trade' misses the broader historical reasoning about patronage patterns.

questions.q: Compare the early stupa at Sanchi (c. 2nd–1st century BCE) with the later Amaravati stupa (c. 2nd century CE) in terms of (i) surface treatment, (ii) narrative content, and (iii) the role of the harmika.
questions.a: (i) Sanchi: plain anda with uncarved railing; Amaravati: elaborately carved dome with narrative bands. (ii) Sanchi: Jataka stories on gateways only; Amaravati: entire drum covered with life-scenes and Jatakas. (iii) Sanchi: harmika intact with yashti/chhatra; Amaravati: harmika often reduced or replaced by a solid cylindrical element. A wrong answer that says 'both are identical' ignores the evolutionary trajectory from symbolic to narrative architecture.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: 'The survival of Sanchi and the near-total loss of Amaravati were primarily due to the differing attitudes of local rulers in the 19th century.' Support with evidence.
questions.a: Partly true: Bhopal begums (Shahjehan Begum, Sultan Jehan Begum) actively funded preservation and blocked removal, while Amaravati was quarried by a local raja and later stripped by British officials (Elliot, Mackenzie) with no protective authority. However, Sanchi's earlier 'discovery' (1818) when three gateways still stood, and H.H. Cole's in-situ advocacy, were equally critical. A one-sided answer blaming only 'British looting' or only 'local neglect' fails to weigh multiple causal factors.

questions.q: Design a museum exhibit panel (150 words) that explains the anda-harmika-yashti-chhatra axis to a visitor unfamiliar with Buddhist cosmology, using only the metaphors of 'cosmic egg', 'heavenly terrace', 'world axis', and 'royal canopy'.
questions.a: A strong panel links: anda = cosmic egg (universe in potential); harmika = heavenly terrace where gods reside; yashti = world axis (Mount Meru) connecting earth and heaven; chhatra = royal canopy marking the Buddha as universal monarch (chakravartin). A weak panel merely lists terms without metaphors or reverses the vertical order.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A stupa is a ______ Buddhist funerary monument originating as a simple earthen mound (anda) enshrining relics of the Buddha or revered monks; it evolved into a complex sacred structure comprising the anda (cosmic egg), harmika (balcony representing the abode of gods), yashti (central mast), chhatra (umbrella symbolizing royalty and the cosmic axis), a vedika (railing demarcating sacred space), and toranas (gateways at cardinal points) — all designed for clockwise circumambulation (pradakshina) as an act of veneration.
Fill in the blank: Imagine standing at ______ station — the train halts for two minutes and you see the Great Stupa crowning the hill.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can label every architectural component of a stupa on a plan and elevation, explain the symbolic meaning of each element using Buddhist cosmology, trace the evolution from Mauryan to post-Mauryan stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati), and interpret donative inscriptions to reconstruct patronage patterns.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A stupa is a hemispherical Buddhist funerary monument originating as a simple earthen mound (anda) enshrining relics of the Buddha or revered monks; it evolved into a complex sacred structure comprising the anda (cosmic egg), harmika (balcony representing the abode of gods), yashti (central mast), chhatra (umbrella symbolizing royalty and the cosmic axis), a vedika (railing demarcating sacred space), and toranas (gateways at cardinal points) — all designed for clockwise ______ (pradakshina) as an act of veneration.
Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ at Sanchi station — the train halts for two minutes and you see the Great Stupa crowning the hill.
